newsitem.title: UK: British budget deficit poised to better forecast.
newsitem.headline: British budget deficit poised to better forecast.

text.p: Britain's budget deficit is likely to be below the Conservative government's forecast in the financial year which ends this month, according to official figures released on Tuesday.

The government, which is trying to trumpet its management of the economy in the run-up to the May 1 election, said the February budget deficit of 3.6 billion pounds ($5.7 billion) showed it had the public finances under control.

The Office for National Statistics (ONS) said the cumulative deficit for the first 11 months of the year was 14.1 billion pounds, well below the 22.2 billion figure recorded in the same period last year.
Economists said the final figure for the financial year would probably be around 24 billion pounds, below the government's projection of 26.4 billion.
"It shows we're on course for the balanced budget that I foresee by the end of the century," finance minister Kenneth Clarke told a news conference.
"It gives the lie to the Labour party's claims that there's any problem with the public finances, which we have under control."
Economists said the government appeared to have kept spending under control, despite the temptation to try to curry favour with voters by boosting spending before the election.

"Coming up to the last election, there was a definite upward trend, but I've got to hand it to them, they've really kept spending under control this time," NatWest Markets economist John O'Sullivan said.
"Given it's an election year, that's an exceptional performance."
Opinion polls suggest the Conservatives are likely to lose the election and relinquish power to the opposition Labour Party.
Economists said even the customary end-of-year rush by government departments to use up their remaining cash would be unlikely to push the full-year budget deficit above the government estimate.
"It's now taken as given that there will be an undershoot of several billion pounds," said David Coleman, chief economist at Canadian bank CIBC.
"The question is now what happens next year," he said, arguing that the new government might not need to borrow as much in the 1997-98 fiscal year as the 19.2 billion projected.
Labour, anxious to shake off its past image as the party of high taxation, has promised not to raise income tax rates and to live within the Conservatives' tight spending limits.
"The fiscal side is looking much rosier for the new government. If you've got a trend improvement in borrowing, it gives them a little bit more room for manoeuvre," Coleman said.

But although the whole year deficit will be lower than the latest official forecast, it is still likely to be almost double the official estimate made two years ago, HSBC economist Jonathan Loynes said.
"We continue to believe that the next government would be well advised to tighten fiscal policy at some point," he said.
"As well as improving the public finances, this could help to ease the upward pressure on sterling by minimizing the need for further rises in interest rates."
